# Fallthrough

> [中文](README.zh.md)

**This project is generated by AI.** The compiler, the standard library, the tests and
this documentation were written by the model **DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017**, running inside
**DeepSeek Harness**. A person directs the design; the model writes the tree.

## A very young language

Fallthrough is at the very beginning. Work started on **2026-10-12**, so the language
is still very young, and everything that follows from that is true:

- **The syntax is not stable.** Keywords, declaration forms and attributes still move.
- **The standard library is not stable.** Modules, types, functions and their signatures
  change between builds; what exists today may be renamed or removed tomorrow.
- **The API and the ABI are not stable.** Aggregate layout, the calling convention and
  the shape of the products are still being decided.
- **The CLI is not stable.** The spelling of options and the set of `--emit=` values may
  change without notice.
- **Generated code is not the best.** The compiler runs no optimisation passes by
  default, so a program is as fast as the code the front end emits; memory use is not
  tuned.
- **There is no compatibility promise.** Until this section disappears, any build may
  break any program. Do not build anything you cannot afford to rewrite on top of it.

For now, this is a toy compiler; in the future, I hope to see it flourish.

## Build speed

A module is compiled once and its products are cached: an interface, the compiled
functions, and the list of templates that go with them. A second build of the same
program reads those instead of reading the sources again.

| program | first build | after the cache is warm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hello world` (`import C`) | 0.13 s | 0.05 s |
| a program that imports the standard library | 8.3 s | 0.56 s |

The first build of a program that imports the standard library is the slow case, and
it is slow for the reason every compiler is: the standard library is 67 modules and
the functions their bodies instantiate have to be compiled once. The cache is what
keeps a program's own edit from paying that again.

## Philosophy

Fallthrough is a statically typed, compiled systems language. Its name states the first
rule: when one `switch` arm ends, control does **not** fall into the next arm. A program
that wants fallthrough writes `fallthrough;`. Nothing happens unless it is written.

That rule generalises into the four ideas the language is built around.

1. **Explicit over implicit.** A program does what it says. The only implicit value
   conversions are a short, listed set -- truthiness, array and function decay, adding
   `const`, the byte-pointer conversion; every other conversion is written `expr as T`.
   There is no garbage collector: lifetimes are lexical, and destruction is a statement
   about the scope, not about a runtime.
2. **Value semantics with deterministic destruction.** A value owns what it holds and is
   destroyed when its scope ends, through `__drop__`. Copying and moving are the type's
   own constructors; `std.move` is how a program says a named value is dying.
3. **Errors are part of the type.** A function that can fail says `except`; a call site
   either handles the exception with `try` or ends the program with `!!`. An exception
   carries a type name and a message. There are no hidden error codes and no unchecked
   exceptions.
4. **A small readable core, features grown in the library.** Generics are type families
   with template parameters, traits are answered structurally at compile time, and
   containers, strings, JSON, TOML, XML, networking and logging are ordinary modules
   written in the language itself. The standard library is not magic; it is the first
   user of the language.

The problem it wants to solve: mainstream systems languages still make a programmer carry
a great deal of accidental complexity -- implicit conversions, silently ignored errors,
hidden control flow, ownership rules that need a lifetime notation. Fallthrough tries to
keep the control of a systems language while making the program read as the sequence of
decisions the author actually made: one meaning per construct, everything visible,
nothing implicit.

## Install and run

The repository is [`MrXie1109/Fallthrough`](https://github.com/MrXie1109/Fallthrough).

### Requirements

| Requirement | Why |
| ----------- | --- |
| A Rust toolchain (edition 2024) | the compiler is a Rust workspace |
| LLVM 18 development files | code generation links against LLVM through `inkwell` |
| A C compiler | the linker *driver*, and any C library a program links against |
| `make` | the build driver has the short names: `make release`, `make install` |

If `llvm-sys` cannot find LLVM, point it at the installation:
`LLVM_SYS_181_PREFIX=/path/to/llvm-18 make release`. On Windows the same value
is set with `set LLVM_SYS_181_PREFIX=C:\Program Files\LLVM` before `make`.

### Clone, build and install

The command line below is the Unix one; [Windows](#windows) has its own, because
the install location, the `sudo` and the shell profile are all different there.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/MrXie1109/Fallthrough.git
cd Fallthrough
make release          # build the compiler with optimisations
sudo make install     # copy it to /usr/local/bin (PREFIX, default /usr/local)
fallc --version
```

`make install PREFIX=$HOME/.local` installs without root, if `~/.local/bin` is on
`PATH`. To remove it again: `sudo make uninstall`.

`make install` also places the standard library in
`/usr/local/share/fallthrough/standard` and writes one environment file,
`/usr/local/etc/fallthrough/env`, that names it:

```sh
export FALLTHROUGH_STANDARD="/usr/local/share/fallthrough/standard"
```

The compiler looks for the library through `FALLTHROUGH_STANDARD`, so add that
line to the profile of the shell so that every session has it. With `bash` and
`zsh`, for the current user:

```sh
echo '. /usr/local/etc/fallthrough/env' >> ~/.bashrc   # or ~/.zshrc
```

with `fish`:

```fish
echo 'source /usr/local/etc/fallthrough/env' >> ~/.config/fish/config.fish
```

For every user of the machine: put the same line in `/etc/profile`. Do not use
`sudo` for these two commands -- they edit your own profile, not root's.

### Windows

Windows has no `/usr/local`, no `sudo` and no shell profile that every shell
reads, so the install is a copy and the variable is set for the user in the
registry.

Build in an environment that has `make`, a C compiler for the linker, and LLVM 18
-- an MSYS2/MINGW64 shell, or a Developer PowerShell with `mingw32-make`:

```sh
make release
```

Then copy the compiler and the library somewhere stable, and set the variable.
In PowerShell, for the current user:

```powershell
$root = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Fallthrough"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "$root\bin" | Out-Null
Copy-Item target\release\fallc.exe "$root\bin\fallc.exe"
Copy-Item standard "$root\standard" -Recurse
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable(
    "FALLTHROUGH_STANDARD", "$root\standard", "User")
$env:FALLTHROUGH_STANDARD = "$root\standard"   # this session
$env:PATH = "$root\bin;$env:PATH"
fallc --version
```

In `cmd.exe`, the same variable, permanently:

```bat
setx FALLTHROUGH_STANDARD "%LOCALAPPDATA%\Fallthrough\standard"
```

`setx` affects new shells only, so open a new terminal (or set `FALLTHROUGH_STANDARD`
in the current one as well) before running `fallc`. Add `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Fallthrough\bin`
to `PATH` through **System Properties → Environment Variables** so that `fallc` is
found by name.

A static or shared library built with `--emit=static` or `--emit=shared` is a
`.a` and a `.dll` on Windows, and linking it needs the same toolchain the
compiler used. The CLI options are the same on every platform.

### Hello, world

Write `hello.ft`:

```ft
import C;

fn main() int {
    C.printf("Hello, world!\n");
    return 0;
}
```

Compile and run:

```sh
fallc hello.ft -o hello
./hello
```

The same program against the language's own library:

```ft
import std;

fn main() int except {
    std.println("Hello, world!")!!;
    return 0;
}
```

`println` can fail, so it is declared `except`: `!!` stops the program and prints the
exception; `try` handles it instead.

`import C;` is the C standard library written in the language; `import std;` is the
language's own library. Both are ordinary modules, imported the same way as a module of
one's own.

An executable is the default product. Other products are asked for with `--emit=`:

```sh
fallc hello.ft --emit=obj    -o hello.o     # one object file
fallc hello.ft --emit=static -o libhello.a  # a static library
fallc hello.ft --emit=shared -o libhello.so # a shared library
fallc hello.ft --emit=llvm   -o hello.ll    # the LLVM IR
```

Several `.ft` files are one program; a `.ftm` file is a module for `import`.

## Repository layout

```
crates/            the compiler: span, diagnostics, lexer, AST, parser, sema, IR, driver
standard/          the standard library and the C bindings, written in Fallthrough
examples/          small programs
docs/              the standard, the library reference and the design record
```

The compiler is one crate per stage, and the stage is the crate's job: `fallc-span` and
`fallc-diag` are the foundation, `fallc-lexer` turns text into tokens, `fallc-parser`
turns tokens into an AST, `fallc-sema` resolves names and checks types, `fallc-ir` lowers
the checked tree straight to LLVM IR, and `fallc` is the only crate that performs I/O.

## Development

The repository is a normal Cargo workspace, and `make` is the short name for the common
tasks: `make help` lists them, `make release` builds, `make install` installs. The
workspace stays compile-time-checked with `make check` and lint-clean with `make clippy`.

Adding a language feature keeps the tree compiling at every step:

1. token kinds in `crates/fallc-lexer/src/token.rs` and the keyword/punctuation tables;
2. AST variants in `crates/fallc-ast/src/node/` **and** the matching arms in
   `crates/fallc-ast/src/visit.rs`;
3. the parsing production in `crates/fallc-parser/src/parser/`, plus operator entries in
   `precedence.rs`;
4. resolution and typing rules in `crates/fallc-sema`;
5. lowering in `crates/fallc-ir/src/codegen/` and the type mapping in
   `crates/fallc-ir/src/types.rs` -- there is no opcode enum to extend: emit LLVM
   instructions directly and let the verifier check the result.

An observable rule is not done until a test pins it and the normative paragraph exists in
`docs/language` -- in both languages, since the pair is the standard.
